name: Ibtihaj Muhammad
summary: The Olympic sabre fencer helped broaden public ideas about who could represent the United States in sport.
biography:
Ibtihaj Muhammad grew up in New Jersey and took up fencing, a sport whose full uniform provided room for her to compete while observing her religious practice. She fenced at Duke University and developed as a sabre specialist. Sabre is a fast discipline in which an attack can be scored with the edge of the blade. Success depends on reacting quickly to distance and timing and knowing when a referee will award priority. Those demands were the day-to-day work behind the visibility she later gained.

In Rio in 2016 Muhammad became the first United States Olympic athlete to compete wearing a hijab. She also helped the American team win bronze in women’s sabre. The team result reflected performances by several fencers across a series of bouts. Museum collections preserve examples of her equipment, making the connection between a national milestone and the objects an athlete needed in order to compete. Her career helped make room for younger athletes to imagine participation without treating their religious clothing as incompatible with elite competition.

summary: She won major tennis championships for Japan and brought a distinctive international identity to the world stage.
biography:
Naomi Osaka was born in Japan to a Japanese mother and a Haitian father and spent much of her childhood in the United States. She represented Japan in international tennis while training and competing on a global circuit. Her first major singles title came at the 2018 U.S. Open, where she defeated Serena Williams in the final. She won the Australian Open a few months later. Those victories established her as a player who could carry powerful serving and baseline hitting through the successive matches of a major tournament.

Osaka won additional singles titles at both the U.S. Open and Australian Open. Her victories at the two hard-court majors show how repeatable her game could be across tournaments held at different points in the season. At the opening ceremony of the Tokyo Games in 2021, she lit the Olympic cauldron. A player whose life crossed countries and family traditions was chosen for one of the most visible roles at an Olympics hosted by Japan, an occasion distinct from any result on the court.

name: Marta Vieira da Silva
summary: Marta developed into one of the most accomplished scorers in international football and helped keep Brazil at the center of the women’s game.
biography:
Marta Vieira da Silva grew up in Alagoas, Brazil, and became known internationally by her first name. She developed as a forward who could both create a chance and finish it. Her dribbling drew defenders out of position, while her ability to pass gave Brazil ways to use the space they left. She competed in club football abroad as well as for the Brazilian national team, moving between playing environments that offered women very different professional opportunities.

Brazil won Olympic silver in 2004 and reached the Women’s World Cup final in 2007. In both cases the results depended on a whole team, but Marta’s performances gave supporters a visible point of connection to the women’s game. Years later she was still part of the squad that won silver in Paris. She also became a goodwill ambassador for UN Women. Her career was a reminder that a country can have a deep football culture and still have to build the opportunities that allow girls and women to participate in it on equal terms.

summary: The Brazilian forward won three men’s World Cups and became one of football’s best-known international figures.
biography:
Edson Arantes do Nascimento, known as Pelé, joined Santos as a teenager and reached Brazil’s national team while still young. At the 1958 World Cup he helped turn an injury-delayed start into a decisive role in the knockout rounds. His goals in the final in Sweden made his composure and inventiveness visible to spectators who rarely saw Brazilian club football. His reputation rested on more than finishing chances: he could move between lines, draw defenders and bring teammates into an attack.

Brazil also won the 1962 tournament, although injury prevented Pelé from continuing after the early matches. His third title came in 1970, when he contributed as a scorer and creator in a team celebrated for its collective play. He later joined the New York Cosmos, bringing a prominent international name to a league seeking a larger audience in the United States. His career shows how international tournaments and touring club teams helped turn the reputation of a player in Brazil into a worldwide conversation about how football could be played.

name: Yusra Mardini
summary: She competed in swimming for the Refugee Olympic Team and used that visibility to advocate for displaced people.
biography:
Yusra Mardini trained as a swimmer in Syria before war forced her family to leave. In 2015 she and her sister Sara traveled toward Europe. When the boat carrying them across the Aegean ran into trouble, the sisters and others entered the water to help keep it moving toward safety. After reaching Germany, Mardini returned to structured swim training. Rebuilding an athletic routine in a new country required access to a pool as well as a coach and the time and stability to train.

In 2016 she swam at Rio as a member of the first Refugee Olympic Team. The team gave athletes displaced from their countries a way to compete without a national delegation that could enter them. Mardini later competed at Tokyo and became a goodwill ambassador for the United Nations refugee agency. Her public role grew out of two parts of her experience that are easily separated in retellings: she had survived a dangerous journey, and she had also spent years developing and sustaining the skills of a competitive swimmer.

name: Tatyana McFadden
summary: She won major wheelchair races on the track and road and challenged barriers to participation in school sports.
biography:
Tatyana McFadden was born in Russia and grew up in the United States after being adopted. She took part in several sports before developing as a wheelchair racer. On the track she learned to accelerate and maneuver in fields where timing and position matter; on the road she had to maintain speed across hills, turns and changing pavement for a much longer distance. Her successes in both settings showed the range of technique and conditioning possible within wheelchair racing.

In 2013 she won the women’s wheelchair races at the Boston, London, Chicago and New York City marathons. She also competed at multiple Paralympic Games and won four gold medals at Rio in 2016. Her career included a dispute over access to school sports in Maryland. Being permitted to take part in school competition mattered for more than one athlete’s results: school programs are often where young people find coaching, peers and a path into organized sport. McFadden’s advocacy helped bring attention to how much can depend on the rules at that level.

name: Jim Thorpe
place: United States and Sac and Fox Nation
summary: The Sac and Fox athlete excelled in the Olympic combined events as well as professional football and baseball.
biography:
Jim Thorpe, a member of the Sac and Fox Nation, became nationally known as an athlete at the Carlisle Indian Industrial School. The school was part of an American system that sought to assimilate Indigenous children, a fact that sits alongside its prominence in early collegiate football. Thorpe excelled in football and track. At the Stockholm Olympics in 1912 he won the pentathlon and decathlon, two combined events that rewarded performance across running, jumping and throwing rather than mastery of one narrow specialty.

Officials later stripped his medals because he had previously been paid to play minor-league baseball under rules that excluded professionals. Thorpe went on to play major-league baseball and professional football. He was the first president of the association that became the National Football League. The Olympic record was restored in stages, and in 2022 the IOC recognized him as the sole winner of both events. The dispute illustrates how amateur rules could punish athletes who earned money playing sports even when their performances in competition were beyond dispute.

name: Roberto Clemente
summary: He became one of baseball’s finest right fielders while publicly challenging how Latino players were treated.
biography:
Roberto Clemente grew up in Puerto Rico and reached the major leagues with the Pittsburgh Pirates in 1955. He became known as a right fielder who could narrow an opponent’s options with his throwing arm. A runner deciding whether to take an extra base had to consider how quickly a ball could reach the infield. Clemente also developed into an accomplished hitter and won several National League batting titles. His long tenure in Pittsburgh made him a central figure in two championship teams.

In 1971 Clemente was named the most valuable player of the World Series. He recorded his three-thousandth major league hit in 1972. Throughout his career he faced stereotyping of Latino players and spoke about how they were treated. He died in a plane crash while accompanying relief supplies for people affected by an earthquake in Nicaragua. The Baseball Hall of Fame elected him the next year through a special election. His memory in baseball is tied to both his precision in the game and the uses he made of his public standing beyond it.

name: Abebe Bikila
summary: He won the men’s Olympic marathon twice, demonstrating the strength of Ethiopian distance running to a global audience.
biography:
Abebe Bikila trained as a runner while serving in Ethiopia’s Imperial Guard. At the Rome Olympic marathon in 1960 he ran barefoot, an unusual sight at the elite level of the race. He stayed with the leaders and then broke away to win. The victory gave Ethiopia its first Olympic gold medal and showed the distance running world that a country with relatively little prior Olympic visibility could produce the best runner in the field. The way Bikila ran captured attention, but his pacing and ability to sustain speed did more to decide the outcome than the absence of shoes.

Four years later he wore shoes in Tokyo and won again, becoming the first runner to win the men’s Olympic marathon twice. Equally striking was the gap he established over the field at the finish. His two victories helped put Ethiopian distance running on the international map. They also illustrated what the marathon rewards: it is possible to run very fast for a short stretch and still lose to someone who understands how to distribute effort over the entire course.

name: George Washington Carver
summary: He taught Southern farmers how to improve depleted soil and find uses for crops other than cotton.
biography:
George Washington Carver was born into slavery in Missouri and pursued an education after emancipation. He studied agriculture at what became Iowa State University and joined Tuskegee Institute in Alabama in 1896. Many farmers there depended on cotton even when repeated planting was exhausting the soil. Carver taught methods that could make farms less dependent on one crop. Rotating cotton with legumes and finding buyers or uses for the alternative crop made economic sense only if families could afford to put the advice into practice.

At Tuskegee he helped take instruction outside the campus, including through a mobile classroom known as the Jesup Wagon. His bulletins described crops that could be grown or prepared using materials farmers could get. His experiments with peanuts and other crops became famous, but treating him as the inventor of peanut butter obscures the problems he was actually solving. The useful question was how to help farm households grow food, maintain soil fertility and earn a living under conditions they had not chosen.

name: Percy Julian
summary: He developed ways to synthesize medically useful compounds and make steroid intermediates from plant material at industrial scale.
biography:
Percy Julian trained as an organic chemist and completed doctoral work in Vienna, taking a route through Europe in part because opportunities for Black chemists were limited in the United States. Back at DePauw University, Julian and Josef Pikl completed a synthesis of physostigmine, a substance used in treating glaucoma. They had to demonstrate that their product was the same compound as the one obtained from the plant. A successful synthesis also showed that chemists could obtain it by a route other than extracting it from seeds.

At the Glidden Company, Julian turned his attention to substances found in soybeans. His team developed ways to turn plant sterols into intermediates useful in producing steroid medicines. The work linked two different problems: devising a chemical transformation and finding a starting material available in large enough quantities to make the process practical. He later founded Julian Laboratories. His career helps explain how laboratory chemistry can affect access to medicine through the choice and cost of raw materials as well as through the identification of a useful compound.

name: Charles Drew
summary: He helped establish reliable methods for processing and storing blood plasma for large transfusion programs.
biography:
Charles Drew trained as a physician and surgeon and undertook research at Columbia University on how blood could be stored for transfusion. He studied work on separating plasma from blood cells and on preserving it under conditions that would make it usable when someone needed it. The challenge was not simply keeping a single container viable in a laboratory. A larger service had to collect donations at different sites, test and process them consistently and get the resulting material to patients safely.

Drew put that knowledge to work in the Blood for Britain project in 1940 and in early American Red Cross blood-bank work. He objected to policies restricting or separating donors by race, a classification with no scientific basis for plasma collection. Later, at Howard University and Freedmen’s Hospital, he trained surgeons. Blood banking was the work of teams rather than one inventor. Drew’s contribution lay in joining a research question about preservation to the practical organization needed to make transfusion available far from the original donor.

name: Ernest Everett Just
summary: He used marine eggs to study how the surface of a cell responds to fertilization and how its environment affects development.
biography:
Ernest Everett Just grew up in South Carolina, attended Dartmouth College and taught at Howard University. During summers he worked at the Marine Biological Laboratory at Woods Hole, where marine organisms provided material for examining the earliest moments of development. He studied what happens at the surface of an egg when it is fertilized. To interpret a change, he also wanted to know whether it belonged to the ordinary development of the egg or was a response to how the investigator had treated it.

Just insisted that laboratory handling and the surrounding medium could alter what researchers saw. His attention to those conditions challenged experiments that tried to reach a broad conclusion about a cell after seriously disturbing it. He worked in European laboratories as well as in the United States, where racism narrowed his research opportunities. His 1939 book on the cell surface consolidated ideas built up through years of observation. The distinction he drew between a biological response and an artifact of handling remains important far beyond the organisms he studied.

name: Marie Maynard Daly
summary: She studied proteins in the cell nucleus and later investigated how diet and cholesterol relate to disease in arteries.
biography:
Marie Maynard Daly studied chemistry at Queens College and New York University before earning a doctorate at Columbia in 1947. She was the first Black woman known to earn a PhD in chemistry in the United States. Her graduate research with Mary Letitia Caldwell focused on enzymes involved in digestion. Later research took her to the Rockefeller Institute, where she examined proteins associated with material in the cell nucleus. At a time when researchers were working out what the nucleus contained, measuring the composition of those proteins was part of determining how cells were organized.

Daly’s later research with Quentin Deming considered cholesterol and its relationship to arterial disease. This work brought chemical measurement to a question about processes that develop over time in a living body. She also taught at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine and supported opportunities for students to study science. Her career links detailed work on the composition of cells with questions about how life at that scale affects the health of an entire person.

name: Patricia Bath
summary: She developed a laser-based instrument for cataract surgery and worked to make eye care reachable in underserved communities.
biography:
Patricia Bath trained in ophthalmology and noticed differences between patients served in Harlem and those who had easier access to medical care. Some avoidable sight loss could be addressed only if patients reached a clinician early enough. Bath helped develop an approach known as community ophthalmology, which brought screening and prevention into the places people lived rather than expecting them to find a specialist on their own. She also helped establish the American Institute for the Prevention of Blindness.

Bath pursued a second problem inside the operating room. A cataract clouds the eye’s lens, and removing it requires precise work on a small and delicate part of the body. Bath developed the Laserphaco approach, which used laser energy to break up cataract material so it could be removed. She obtained a U.S. patent in 1988. Her career makes clear why new instruments and better access belong in the same account of public health: a treatment can work in the hands of a surgeon and still make little difference to someone who cannot get an examination or referral.

name: Kizzmekia Corbett
summary: She helped lead coronavirus vaccine research at NIH that informed the development of Moderna’s COVID-19 vaccine.
biography:
Kizzmekia Corbett studied the immune response to viruses before joining the Vaccine Research Center at the U.S. National Institutes of Health. The researchers there had been investigating coronaviruses before the virus that causes COVID-19 appeared. Their earlier work mattered because the new emergency demanded a rapid response, but a candidate vaccine was still the product of experiments that had taken years. Corbett’s team contributed research on the coronavirus spike protein as a target for the immune system.

The NIH scientists worked with Moderna and others to develop and assess a vaccine. Laboratory researchers, clinical investigators, trial participants and manufacturing teams each supplied a different part of the evidence and production needed to make it available. Corbett also spoke to audiences outside the laboratory about what vaccine studies could show and why trust could not simply be assumed during a public health emergency. She later joined the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. Her role illustrates why research between outbreaks, large-scale collaboration and public explanation all matter in responding to a new disease.

name: Jennifer Doudna
summary: Her work with Emmanuelle Charpentier showed how a bacterial defense system could be adapted as a tool for genome editing.
biography:
Jennifer Doudna trained as a biochemist studying RNA, a molecule that can carry information and also perform work inside cells. At the University of California, Berkeley, her laboratory examined how RNA adopts shapes that help it interact with other molecules. Those interests led her to an unusual feature of bacteria: they can preserve information about past encounters with viruses and use it in defending themselves during later encounters.

Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier brought complementary experience to studying one of these systems. In work published in 2012, their teams showed that RNA could guide the Cas9 enzyme to selected DNA sequences. This converted an observation about microbial defense into a tool that researchers could direct toward a question of their own. The two scientists shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Doudna also took part in public discussion about the limits that should apply to human uses of genome editing. The ability to make an alteration raised decisions about consent, evidence and risk that could not be answered by demonstrating that the tool worked.

name: Emmanuelle Charpentier
summary: Her investigations of bacterial RNA helped reveal how CRISPR-Cas9 works and how it could be redirected for research.
biography:
Emmanuelle Charpentier trained in microbiology and studied the interaction between bacteria and their surroundings. She became interested in small RNA molecules that influence what happens inside a bacterial cell. Working with a bacterium that can cause disease in humans, her group identified an RNA involved in a defense system that protects microbes against viruses. The finding explained part of how the system prepares the information it needs to recognize an invader.

Collaboration with Jennifer Doudna and their colleagues showed that the Cas9 enzyme could be directed by RNA to a chosen sequence of DNA. The experiments treated the bacterial machinery as something whose parts could be examined separately, allowing the researchers to understand what made it act at a particular location. Charpentier and Doudna shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Charpentier’s route to the discovery is important because it began with the behavior of bacteria rather than a plan to engineer other organisms. A careful account of a process in microbes supplied the ideas needed for tools with much broader uses in research.

name: Ada Yonath
summary: She helped determine the structure of the ribosome, making it possible to see how some antibiotics interfere with protein production.
biography:
Ada Yonath studied chemistry and biochemistry in Jerusalem and trained in X-ray crystallography at the Weizmann Institute. She chose to investigate the ribosome, the large assembly that uses information carried by RNA to make proteins. Structural work on it demanded a kind of order that the material did not readily provide. Researchers needed crystals whose repeating arrangement would produce an interpretable diffraction pattern, even though the ribosome is built from many parts and can be difficult to keep intact.

Yonath worked over many years to prepare suitable material and to collect data from it. Research on ribosomes from organisms able to live under demanding conditions provided one route toward more stable samples. Structures worked out by several laboratories changed what biologists could see about how the ribosome functions. They also helped explain why some antibiotics can interrupt protein production in bacteria. Yonath shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Venkatraman Ramakrishnan and Thomas Steitz. She had persisted with a method that required solving several practical problems before the original biological question could even be addressed.

name: Elizabeth Blackburn
summary: Her research helped explain how telomeres protect chromosome ends and how cells maintain them.
biography:
Elizabeth Blackburn grew up in Australia and pursued research in molecular biology before working in the United States. A linear chromosome poses a problem that a circular piece of DNA does not: the ends must be maintained through repeated rounds of copying, and the cell must distinguish a natural end from a break that needs repair. Blackburn studied the repetitive DNA at those ends, known as telomeres, in an organism that offered a useful way to examine them.

Her collaborations showed that telomere sequences helped protect chromosome ends. Working with Carol Greider, Blackburn identified an activity that could add new repeats, explaining how some cells maintain them. Blackburn, Greider and Jack Szostak shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Their studies put a mechanism behind observations about the behavior of chromosome ends, opening avenues for research on cell division, aging and cancer. The discovery also illustrates what can come from choosing an organism for the experimental access it offers: a question about the life of cells in general could be approached through detailed work on a microscopic organism.

name: Barbara McClintock
summary: By following inheritance in maize, she found evidence that genetic elements can move and change how traits appear.
biography:
Barbara McClintock trained at Cornell and became exceptionally skilled at identifying chromosomes in maize under a microscope. Because changes in maize kernels could be compared with changes she saw in chromosomes, the plants gave her a way to observe both the outcome of inheritance and some of the physical events that produced it. At Cold Spring Harbor she investigated unstable patterns of pigment, a problem that required following plants and their descendants rather than relying on one generation of results.

McClintock concluded that certain genetic elements could change their position and affect the expression of nearby genes. This challenged the expectation that the locations of genes were largely fixed from one cell generation to another. Other researchers did not immediately appreciate the general significance of the work. Later discoveries of mobile genetic elements in other organisms offered an independent context for understanding her observations. She received the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Her achievement depended on reading the fine detail of inheritance through a combination of careful growing, observation and interpretation.

name: Gerty Cori
summary: Her work with Carl Cori clarified how muscles and the liver exchange and store fuel.
biography:
Gerty Cori studied medicine in Prague and moved with Carl Cori to the United States. The two investigated how the body makes stored carbohydrate available as fuel. A muscle doing intense work can produce lactate, and the lactate can travel to the liver, where its carbon is used to make glucose again. Understanding that exchange allowed researchers to see the liver and muscles as parts of a linked system rather than independent consumers of fuel.

The Coris also studied the enzymes involved in forming and breaking down glycogen, the form in which animals store much of their carbohydrate. Gerty Cori’s work later connected defects in particular enzymes with patterns of abnormal glycogen storage. She had long faced unequal professional treatment even when her work was central to a shared research program. In 1947 the Coris and Bernardo Houssay shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. The research showed how chemical reactions in different tissues work together to keep fuel available when a body’s immediate needs change.

name: Dorothy Hodgkin
summary: She used X-ray crystallography to determine the structures of medically important molecules including penicillin, vitamin B12 and insulin.
biography:
Dorothy Hodgkin studied chemistry at Oxford and learned to use X-ray diffraction to infer how atoms are arranged inside a crystal. A pattern of spots does not look like a picture of a molecule. Researchers have to interpret the strength and position of the spots and test whether a proposed arrangement accounts for what they measure. Hodgkin applied that method to substances whose structures were difficult to settle by the usual chemical approaches.

During the Second World War she worked with collaborators to resolve the structure of penicillin. She later determined the structure of vitamin B12, a molecule with many atoms arranged around cobalt. The 1964 Nobel Prize in Chemistry recognized her use of diffraction to work out such structures. Her long-running investigation of insulin reached a solution with her team in 1969. The recurring point of the work was to connect the behavior of a substance to the arrangement of its atoms. Determining that arrangement gave other scientists and physicians a more precise object of study than a chemical formula alone.

name: Gertrude Elion
summary: She helped develop medicines by looking for differences in the way healthy cells and their targets use chemical building blocks.
biography:
Gertrude Elion studied chemistry before taking a research position at Burroughs Wellcome, where she worked with George Hitchings. Their approach began with questions about the ways cells make and use the building blocks of DNA and RNA. A useful medicine might interfere with a process that a disease-causing organism or a rapidly growing cell relied on, while doing less damage to other cells in the body. That idea gave researchers a reason to make particular compounds and compare how they acted, rather than test candidates with no account of why they might work.

Work by the teams Elion helped lead contributed to treatments for leukemia and to medicines used to suppress immune rejection after transplantation. At the same laboratory she directed work that produced acyclovir, a treatment for infections caused by herpes viruses. Elion shared the 1988 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Hitchings and James Black. In her career, the contribution was as much about how to choose what to test as it was about any one medicine that ultimately succeeded.

name: Françoise Barré-Sinoussi
summary: She helped identify HIV and later connected laboratory research with international efforts to prevent and treat infection.
biography:
Françoise Barré-Sinoussi trained in research on retroviruses at the Institut Pasteur in Paris. In the early years of the AIDS epidemic, physicians and researchers were trying to find out what caused a collapse of the immune system in people whose symptoms could be very different. Barré-Sinoussi worked with a team investigating samples sent by clinicians. Her experience helped the researchers recognize evidence of a retrovirus in material from a patient. The group reported its finding in 1983, and subsequent work by several teams established the connection between the virus and AIDS.

A laboratory finding created opportunities for testing and research, but it did not settle questions about who could obtain a diagnosis or treatment. Barré-Sinoussi continued her research and took part in international efforts linking scientists, clinicians and communities affected by HIV. She shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Luc Montagnier and Harald zur Hausen. Her part in the history of HIV shows how quickly a laboratory question can become inseparable from decisions about access to health care.

name: May-Britt Moser
summary: She helped discover grid cells, which reveal how the brain organizes information about location.
biography:
May-Britt Moser studied psychology and neuroscience in Norway and became interested in how a brain keeps track of where an animal is. The question can be studied by comparing an animal’s movement with the activity of individual neurons. A researcher then has to work out whether patterns in the firing of those neurons track a feature of the animal’s surroundings or a regularity in the positions it visits. Moser and her colleagues recorded such patterns while animals moved through an enclosure.

Their report in 2005 described cells that fired at multiple positions arranged like the points of a triangular grid. These grid cells appeared in a region of the brain that exchanges information with the hippocampus. The result gave researchers a way to investigate how position and movement are represented together. May-Britt Moser shared the 2014 Nobel Prize with Edvard Moser and John O’Keefe. Their discoveries made spatial navigation accessible as an experimental problem about interactions among populations of cells, rather than only as a description of behavior.

name: Christiane Nüsslein-Volhard
summary: She and Eric Wieschaus used fruit fly genetics to work out how genes organize the early form of an animal.
biography:
Christiane Nüsslein-Volhard studied biochemistry and became interested in how an embryo takes on an organized shape. A young fruit fly develops repeated segments in a predictable order. She and Eric Wieschaus asked what would happen to those patterns if particular genes stopped working. Instead of choosing only a few examples, they examined many lines of flies and sorted the defects they found. The resulting patterns helped them distinguish genes that affect large regions from genes involved in organizing smaller, repeated parts.

The study, published in 1980, showed that the visible structure of the embryo could be used to reconstruct an order of events controlled by genes. Other researchers were able to compare parts of that system with ones in other animals. Nüsslein-Volhard later pursued developmental questions in zebrafish. She shared the 1995 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Wieschaus and Edward Lewis. A durable part of her contribution was demonstrating the value of a systematic search that could reveal important genes before anybody knew what each one did.

name: Donna Strickland
summary: With Gérard Mourou, she developed a way to produce intense, brief laser pulses without damaging the equipment that amplifies them.
biography:
Donna Strickland studied engineering physics in Canada before pursuing doctoral work at the University of Rochester. She and Gérard Mourou set out to make extremely intense pulses of laser light. Simply amplifying a very short pulse can put too much power through an optical component at one time and damage it. Their solution was to spread the pulse out in time, amplify it while its peak power was lower, and then compress it.

Strickland and Mourou published their demonstration in 1985. The method is called chirped pulse amplification because it uses differences among the frequencies in a pulse to change its duration. It became important in laboratories studying the interaction of light and matter and in applications requiring very precise delivery of energy. Strickland later carried out research and taught at the University of Waterloo. She shared the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physics. The innovation came from treating a problem of timing separately from one of amplification, giving researchers access to pulses that their equipment could not have produced by a straightforward increase in power.

name: Andrea Ghez
summary: Her team tracked stars near the center of the Milky Way and provided strong evidence for a supermassive black hole.
biography:
Andrea Ghez trained in astronomy and began using the Keck telescopes in Hawaiʻi to observe stars near the center of the Milky Way. That region is difficult to study in visible light because dust lies between it and Earth. Infrared observations offered access, but images also needed to be sharp enough to distinguish stars crowded together in the sky. Ghez and her collaborators used observing and image-processing methods that reduced the blurring caused by the atmosphere.

The researchers returned to the same stars over many years. By measuring changes in position and velocity, they could constrain the amount of mass inside the stars’ orbits. Several million Suns’ worth of mass appeared to be concentrated in a very small space, consistent with a supermassive black hole. Independent research led by Reinhard Genzel reached a similar conclusion. Ghez shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics. Her achievement depended as much on continuity as on a new observation: what revealed the unseen object was how the visible stars moved over years.

name: Anne L’Huillier
summary: Her work on the interaction of lasers and gases helped make attosecond pulses of light possible.
biography:
Anne L’Huillier trained in physics in France and investigated how intense laser light interacts with atoms. When a laser passes through a gas under suitable conditions, the light that comes out can contain frequencies far above the original one. In experiments begun in the 1980s, L’Huillier and her colleagues observed an unexpected distribution of these higher frequencies. Understanding the pattern required explaining how an electron in an atom responds as the intense light field changes over a very short interval.

The higher frequencies were also useful because their light could be combined to produce extremely brief bursts. At Lund University, L’Huillier continued investigating how to generate and use those pulses. A pulse lasting attoseconds offers an experimental interval short enough to study changes in the behavior of electrons, rather than only the slower motion of atoms or whole structures. L’Huillier shared the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physics with Pierre Agostini and Ferenc Krausz. Their contributions show how explaining a surprising result in one experiment can create the measuring tool for another field of investigation.

name: Maria Goeppert Mayer
summary: She developed a model that explained why some arrangements of protons and neutrons make unusually stable atomic nuclei.
biography:
Maria Goeppert Mayer trained in physics in Göttingen and moved to the United States, where academic restrictions and hiring customs left her working for long periods without a regular paid faculty position. During and after the Second World War she took part in research at several institutions. At Argonne National Laboratory and the University of Chicago she pursued a pattern in the data on atomic nuclei. Certain numbers of protons or neutrons occurred in especially stable nuclei, but researchers needed a reason those numbers kept appearing.

Mayer proposed that protons and neutrons fill groups of energy states inside a nucleus. The groups are called shells. A key part of the model was the effect of the interaction between a particle’s spin and its motion within the nucleus. Hans Jensen and colleagues developed a similar account independently. Mayer and Jensen shared the 1963 Nobel Prize in Physics with Eugene Wigner. The shell model made it possible to connect recurring patterns in nuclear data with an arrangement of particles that could not otherwise be seen.

name: Maria Mitchell
summary: She discovered a comet in 1847 and made direct observation central to astronomy teaching at Vassar.
biography:
Maria Mitchell grew up in Nantucket, Massachusetts, where her father taught her to observe the sky and work with instruments used to keep time and aid navigation. Routine observations taught her to recognize familiar objects and spot something that did not belong in its usual place. In 1847 she saw a comet through a telescope and recorded what she found. Recognition of the discovery gave her international visibility at a time when women had few routes into professional astronomy.

Mitchell later joined the original faculty of Vassar College. She brought students into the observatory to work with instruments and participate in observations themselves. This approach took time and required access to facilities, neither of which women studying science could always count on. Mitchell used her position to advocate for greater educational and professional opportunities for women. Her work at Vassar shows a second way to affect astronomy beyond a notable discovery: teach people how to make and record observations so they are equipped to identify discoveries of their own.

name: Caroline Herschel
summary: She discovered comets and turned thousands of astronomical observations into catalogs useful to other observers.
biography:
Caroline Herschel grew up in Hanover and moved to England to join her brother William. She trained as a singer before the siblings turned much of their attention to astronomy. During observing sessions she recorded and organized measurements, and she used a telescope to search the sky herself. A comet is difficult to recognize in a single observation: an observer can check whether an object moves and compare its position with the stars in repeated views. In 1786 she reported her first comet discovery.

Herschel also produced reference work that made earlier observations easier to use. Catalogs had to reconcile entries made at different times and help an astronomer tell whether an object had already been recorded. After William’s death she continued to organize material from their work. The Royal Astronomical Society awarded her its Gold Medal in 1828. Her career shows why cataloging and discovery should not be treated as opposites. A reliable record of what others have seen gives each new observer a better chance of recognizing what is genuinely new.

name: Henrietta Swan Leavitt
summary: Her work on variable stars provided the relationship astronomers needed to use some stars as distance markers.
biography:
Henrietta Swan Leavitt worked at the Harvard College Observatory, where women examined photographic plates and made measurements needed for larger research programs. She compared images of the Magellanic Clouds taken at different times. A star on one plate could appear brighter or fainter on another, so finding variable stars required comparing many plates rather than examining an isolated image. Leavitt concentrated on the rate at which some of those stars became brighter and dimmer.

In the Small Magellanic Cloud, the stars she compared were far enough away that differences in their distances from Earth were small relative to the overall distance. That made it possible to distinguish differences due to the stars themselves. Cepheid variables that reached greater brightness tended to take longer to complete a cycle. Leavitt’s 1912 publication described this relation. Once other astronomers calibrated it, they could compare a Cepheid’s expected brightness with how bright it looked and estimate its distance. The method extended the reach of observations much farther than direct geometric measurements could go at the time.

name: Mary Anning
summary: Her fossil discoveries along the Dorset coast helped reveal the diversity of ancient marine reptiles.
biography:
Mary Anning learned to find fossils on the coast around Lyme Regis, where waves and landslides expose new material to anyone willing to examine the cliffs and shore. Fossil collecting brought income to her family as well as contact with people studying the history of life. As a girl she helped recover an ichthyosaur skeleton after her brother Joseph found its skull. Anning continued to recognize specimens that could easily have been passed over as pieces of rock, and she became skilled at removing them without losing important details.

In 1823 she discovered a nearly complete plesiosaur. Its proportions were unlike those of animals familiar to most naturalists in Britain. Other finds added evidence that ancient seas and coastlines supported forms of life that no longer existed. Anning dealt with collectors and specialists even though women could not participate in many of the institutions that accredited their work. Her career explains why the discovery, preparation and interpretation of a fossil can be distinct jobs, and why a person on the shore was essential to questions later debated in museums and learned societies.

name: Eunice Foote
summary: Her 1856 experiments compared how gases warmed in sunlight and led her to consider how carbon dioxide might affect climate.
biography:
Eunice Foote lived in New York and took part in the women’s rights convention at Seneca Falls in 1848. She also performed experiments with readily available equipment. In a study published in 1856, Foote compared the temperatures of cylinders containing different gases after placing them in sunlight. A cylinder with carbon dioxide warmed strongly and cooled more slowly under her experimental conditions. She used the result to consider what might happen if the atmosphere had once contained more of that gas.

Her work should be distinguished from later experiments that isolated the absorption of infrared radiation more directly. The apparatus could have captured several effects at once. What Foote established was a measurable difference under her test conditions, from which she drew an unusually early connection to atmospheric temperature. Her paper was communicated at a scientific meeting without her presenting it herself. The study’s later recovery has helped historians distinguish the development of a scientific idea from the process by which particular experiments and investigators became widely known.

name: Rachel Carson
summary: Her writing made the ecological consequences of indiscriminate pesticide use a subject of public debate.
biography:
Rachel Carson studied biology and worked for the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. She learned to write for readers who might never see a scientific journal and applied that skill to subjects ranging from the movement of the oceans to the life of a shore. A reader could follow her accounts of the sea through ordinary observations without losing sight of the larger processes connecting living things. The success of her books gave her an audience for a more contested question.

In Silent Spring, published in 1962, Carson brought together evidence about the effects of widespread pesticide use. A chemical intended to control one species might reach others through soil, water or food. Carson asked readers to consider what happened beyond the immediate goal of applying it and challenged the assumption that spraying should be chosen without examining alternatives. The book generated criticism from industry and became part of a public debate that contributed to changes in pesticide regulation. Carson’s influence depended on making evidence about connections among organisms legible to people making decisions outside a laboratory.

name: Sylvia Earle
summary: She used prolonged underwater observation to study marine life and made ocean protection a public cause.
biography:
Sylvia Earle trained as a marine botanist and became interested in observing ocean life where it grows. Collecting a specimen is useful, but it can reveal little about what an organism does over the course of a day or how it interacts with a living community. Earle used diving and underwater equipment to extend the time researchers could spend making those observations. In the Tektite II project in 1970, she led a team of women who lived and worked in an underwater habitat.

Earle also worked with people designing deep-sea equipment, helping bring scientific questions into decisions about how observation vehicles should be built. She served as chief scientist at the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Later public efforts used what she had seen at sea to argue for protecting particular marine places. Her career connects access and conservation. Better instruments make it possible to discover ecological relationships in places most people never visit, while sustained public work gives those observations a chance to influence which places are protected.

name: Jane Goodall
summary: Her long field study of chimpanzees at Gombe changed how scientists understood their behavior and supported later conservation work.
biography:
Jane Goodall went to Gombe, in what is now Tanzania, to observe chimpanzees in their habitat. At first the animals kept their distance, and she had to spend long periods watching and waiting. The extended contact eventually let her recognize individuals and observe changes over time. In 1960 she saw chimpanzees modify and use plant material to obtain termites. The observation drew attention because making and using tools had often been treated as a defining human activity.

Subsequent study at Gombe recorded social relationships, care of young, conflict and other behavior rarely visible during short visits. Goodall later founded an institute that supported research and conservation. That work connected the animals’ prospects with the circumstances of people living nearby, whose choices are shaped by their own need for land and livelihoods. The value of Gombe lay in the continuity of observation as well as in the original findings. Later researchers could ask questions that became possible only after many years of reliable records.

name: Louis Armstrong
summary: His trumpet playing and singing helped make the individual solo central to jazz.
biography:
Louis Armstrong grew up in New Orleans, where parades, dances and neighborhood bands gave him opportunities to hear different ways of playing. He learned cornet as a young man and eventually went to Chicago to join King Oliver. Armstrong’s playing drew attention for its timing and its ability to give a musical phrase a recognizable shape. A solo could take the place of a sung story, with its own hesitations, emphases and climactic notes, even when the melody belonged to a familiar song.

His Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings gave listeners an extended opportunity to hear that approach. They helped establish a model in which an improvising soloist could come forward without losing the support and response of the band. Armstrong used similar rhythmic freedom as a singer and reached audiences outside jazz clubs through tours, broadcasts and films. His influence can still be heard where musicians place a note slightly ahead of or behind the beat in order to express something a printed melody cannot specify.

name: Duke Ellington
summary: He composed for the distinctive sound of his orchestra’s musicians and extended what a jazz band could do.
biography:
Edward Kennedy Ellington grew up in Washington, D.C., and pursued music as a pianist and bandleader. In New York, the orchestra he led developed a sound built from the personalities of its players. Ellington could write a passage with a particular tone or phrasing in mind because he knew who would play it. The group’s association with the Cotton Club and radio broadcasts widened its audience. That visibility coexisted with the racial restrictions of a segregated entertainment industry.

Ellington and his longtime collaborator Billy Strayhorn wrote and arranged music that ranged from short pieces to extended works. Black, Brown and Beige, presented at Carnegie Hall in 1943, used the orchestra to address Black American history across a longer musical span. The band made changes in personnel, settings and audiences over decades. The distinctive quality of its work came from treating instrumental colors as compositional material. A melody did not have to sound the same simply because it used the same notes; Ellington could make the choice of player part of the musical idea itself.

name: Ella Fitzgerald
summary: She became an influential interpreter of American popular song and helped establish scat singing as an expressive jazz practice.
biography:
Ella Fitzgerald won an amateur competition at Harlem’s Apollo Theater as a young singer and went on to sing with Chick Webb’s orchestra. The band gave her experience performing with arrangements written for dancers and making a vocal line stand out among other instruments. She became its leader after Webb died. Her recordings later showed how comfortably her voice could alternate between telling the story of a song and improvising with a freedom more often associated with a saxophone or trumpet.

Fitzgerald was especially admired for scat singing, using syllables without a fixed text to build melodies and rhythms of her own. Beginning in the 1950s, she also made a series of songbook recordings, devoting whole albums to composers and lyricists. Those records preserve the clarity of her diction and her respect for the written song without sacrificing the flexibility she brought to jazz. What connects the two kinds of work is her control of musical time: both a familiar lyric and an improvised line could become more expressive through the way she delivered it.

name: Marian Anderson
summary: The contralto’s performances became occasions to challenge racial barriers at major American concert and opera venues.
biography:
Marian Anderson began singing in Philadelphia and developed a concert repertory that included European art songs and spirituals. Audiences abroad and at home heard a contralto able to sustain a quiet musical line as well as fill a large hall. Success as a touring artist did not grant her access to every venue in the United States. In 1939 the Daughters of the American Revolution refused to let her sing at Constitution Hall because she was Black.

Anderson instead sang at the Lincoln Memorial before a large crowd, and radio carried the performance to many others. The concert mattered because an exclusion that could have remained administrative became public, while Anderson was heard seriously as a musician. In 1955 she made her Metropolitan Opera debut, becoming the first Black performer to sing with the company. These events opened possibilities for later singers, but they are also episodes from an extensive musical career. Anderson’s artistry gave the movement for access a compelling reason to insist that an audience should be able to hear her.

name: Paul Robeson
summary: The singer and actor used his international standing to speak about racism, workers’ rights and colonialism.
biography:
Paul Robeson studied at Rutgers University, where he achieved distinction in football and in the classroom, and earned a law degree at Columbia. He made his career in the arts. The musical qualities of his deep voice brought him to concerts and recordings, while his work on stage included productions that confronted racial inequality. In 1943 he took the title role in Othello on Broadway. The part gave a Black actor the opportunity to portray a character that American productions had often assigned to white actors.

Robeson’s international career also made it possible for him to speak about racism, labor and colonialism to audiences in several countries. His political positions brought intense scrutiny in the United States during the Cold War. For years the government kept him from traveling abroad by denying him a passport. The restriction made clear how closely his work as an artist depended on the ability to move and perform. Recordings and evidence of his performances preserve the range of a career sometimes remembered only for the controversy that surrounded it.

name: Josephine Baker
summary: She built a career on the Paris stage, supported the French Resistance and later spoke at the March on Washington.
biography:
Josephine Baker grew up in St. Louis and found work in American performance troupes before going to Paris in 1925. A revue there gave her a stage on which quick changes of movement, comic timing and a strong sense of how to hold an audience made her a star. French audiences sometimes interpreted her performances through their own racial fantasies. Baker had to work within those expectations while making decisions about her image and expanding the range of parts she could play.

During the Second World War she used her ability to move within social and professional circles to assist the French Resistance. She later spoke openly against segregation in the United States and appeared at the 1963 March on Washington. Her life connects work usually described separately: performing for an audience and using the relationships or mobility that a career can make possible. Her contributions to France during the war and her civil rights advocacy cannot be accounted for by her fame alone, but that fame gave her opportunities to act.

name: Celia Cruz
summary: She helped carry Cuban musical traditions into the international salsa scene and became one of its defining singers.
biography:
Celia Cruz grew up in Havana and developed her voice through Cuban radio and live performance. Joining La Sonora Matancera in 1950 brought her to audiences across Latin America. Cruz learned to make a vocal line cut through percussion and brass without losing a close connection to the rhythm. The lively exchange between a lead singer and the chorus gave her room to vary a phrase while making it easy for listeners to follow the song.

Cruz left Cuba with the group and built a recording career abroad. In the United States she worked with several bandleaders, including Tito Puente and Johnny Pacheco. Her collaboration with Pacheco, Celia & Johnny, became a landmark of the salsa boom. Salsa was a scene shaped by many communities and musical traditions, so Cruz’s contribution is best heard in how she brought her experience with Cuban music into that changing setting. A singer recognizable from the first few notes could connect audiences separated by migration, national boundaries and different ways of naming the music they shared.

name: Odetta
summary: She brought spirituals, blues and work songs to new audiences and performed in support of the civil rights movement.
biography:
Odetta Holmes was born in Alabama and grew up in California. She received training in classical singing and worked in theater before pursuing folk music. That foundation gave her a powerful voice, but the force of her performances also came from choices about pace and emphasis. In singing a work song or a spiritual, she could let a repeated phrase accumulate meaning from one line to the next. Her guitar accompanied a voice that gave listeners time to hear the history and feeling contained in the material.

Her recordings helped shape the American folk revival. The songs drew on several traditions and were not created for the commercial setting in which some listeners first heard them. Odetta brought that material into concerts without making it an artifact of the past. She also performed at the March on Washington in 1963. Her career shows why music could matter to a movement even when it was not a statement of policy: it gave people a way to remember struggle and hear their own hopes represented in a public gathering.

name: Mercedes Sosa
summary: She brought socially engaged Latin American songs to large audiences and kept performing through censorship and exile.
biography:
Mercedes Sosa grew up in Tucumán, in northwestern Argentina, and began performing music rooted in regional traditions. She later joined artists who promoted the Nuevo Cancionero, a movement that argued for keeping those traditions alive by allowing them to address the problems of the present. Sosa’s deep voice carried songs about poverty, belonging and political violence into concert halls. She could give a line a sense of intimacy even in a performance for a large audience.

During Argentina’s military dictatorship, censorship and repression limited what artists could perform and put Sosa herself at risk. She spent time in exile and returned to give concerts in Argentina in 1982. Her repertory extended well beyond Argentina, drawing from writers and musicians elsewhere in Latin America. This reach mattered because the same song could take on different meanings depending on who was listening and what they had experienced. Sosa connected those audiences through performance, making music a place to express feelings that public institutions had often tried to suppress.

name: Umm Kulthum
summary: Her concerts and broadcasts helped make modern Arabic song a shared experience across national borders.
biography:
Umm Kulthum grew up in rural Egypt and learned to sing in a family whose repertory included religious material. After moving to Cairo, she worked with poets and composers as her performances reached larger audiences. She was known for a voice that could sustain a phrase and for a willingness to change its course while singing. A repeated line could be varied in pitch, ornament or emphasis until the audience heard a different feeling in the same words.

Broadcasts took the experience of her concerts far beyond the venue. Listeners across the Arabic-speaking world could follow a performance at the same time, even if they were listening in different countries or had never seen her on stage. Songs associated with major composers and poets gained a distinctive life in her performances. Her career shows how radio could circulate a demanding art rather than require it to become shorter or simpler. Even listeners far from Cairo could attend closely to the choices she made while developing a long song.

name: Hokusai
summary: His woodblock prints made landscapes into an independent subject of great variety and influenced artists outside Japan.
biography:
Katsushika Hokusai trained in Japan’s woodblock-print culture, where an image passed through the hands of designers, carvers and printers before it reached a buyer. Across a long career he made studies of everyday movement, illustrated books and designed landscapes. His series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji places the mountain in changing weather and surroundings. Sometimes it dominates a scene. In other prints a form closer to the viewer occupies much more of the image, leaving the mountain small in the distance.

Under the Wave off Kanagawa, commonly called The Great Wave, uses the boats and curling water to make that relationship dramatic. The mountain gives the eye a fixed point beyond the danger in the foreground. The print was made to circulate in multiples, and prints by Hokusai later reached collectors and artists in other countries. His influence is not limited to one famous wave. A series built from variations on one subject lets viewers compare how viewpoint, scale and the work of a few lines change what an image makes them notice.

name: Jacob Lawrence
summary: His painted series used repeated forms, colors and captions to tell the story of the Great Migration.
biography:
Jacob Lawrence grew up in Harlem and studied art in a neighborhood with workshops, libraries and artists who made Black history part of their shared work. He developed a practice of telling a story through several paintings. A single panel could show an ordinary event, such as waiting on a platform, while the sequence connected it to large changes in where people lived and worked. Lawrence carried shapes and colors across the series so that the panels belonged to one work even when the subjects changed.

The Migration Series consists of sixty panels about the movement of African Americans from the rural South to cities in the North. Its short captions help readers connect an individual image with a historical circumstance such as labor demand or violence. The paintings were acquired by two museums, and exhibitions that reunite them allow visitors to follow the sequence. Lawrence also taught for many years. His work demonstrates that visual art can explain a sustained historical process without treating the people pictured as anonymous figures in a diagram.

name: Elizabeth Catlett
summary: Her prints and sculptures used familiar forms and working people’s lives to address racism and economic inequality.
biography:
Elizabeth Catlett studied at Howard University and developed her practice as a sculptor at the University of Iowa. She became interested in making art whose subjects looked like people she knew and whose meaning could be understood outside a private collection. Different media gave her different ways to do this. A sculpture could convey weight and steadiness through the contour of a body, while a relief print could be produced in multiple impressions and reach people who might never see the original block.

Catlett moved to Mexico and worked with the Taller de Gráfica Popular, a collective whose artists made prints about social issues and working life. Her images of women and families drew on experiences and traditions on both sides of the border. Political pressure also restricted her ability to travel back to the United States for a period. Her art made room for recognizable lives without limiting those lives to an illustration of hardship. Figures in her work could occupy the center of the image on their own terms.

name: Augusta Savage
summary: She created sculpture during the Harlem Renaissance and helped make training and studio space available to other artists.
biography:
Augusta Savage made sculpture as a child in Florida and pursued formal training after moving to New York. She became part of a network of artists and teachers in Harlem. Her sculpture Gamin is a portrait bust of a boy, with a tilted cap and an expression that gives a small work a distinct personality. The sensitivity of the modeling helped win recognition, although finding enough money to cast or preserve works remained difficult throughout her career.

Savage saw training and space as problems that could be solved collectively. She taught and helped develop community art programs in Harlem. The 1939 New York World’s Fair commissioned her to create The Harp, a large work in which a row of singers becomes the strings of a musical instrument. It was destroyed after the fair, as happened to many works made for temporary exhibitions. Photographs and smaller surviving sculptures must carry much of the evidence of her practice. Her role as a teacher survives in a different way, through opportunities she made possible for artists whose work otherwise might not have developed.

name: Tarsila do Amaral
summary: Her paintings helped Brazilian modernists develop an approach rooted in their own country’s landscapes and visual culture.
biography:
Tarsila do Amaral studied painting in Brazil and France and worked with artists and writers examining what modern art in Brazil could be. European training offered techniques, but also raised a question about whose places and experiences counted as subjects for new art. A trip through Minas Gerais reinforced her interest in the colors, forms and buildings she recognized in Brazil. She developed ways to simplify a landscape while keeping it recognizable as a place that mattered to her.

In Abaporu, painted in 1928, a large figure with an oversized foot appears beside a cactus. The painting became associated with the Anthropophagic movement, which used the metaphor of consuming and transforming outside influences rather than merely copying them. Tarsila later made work on subjects including workers and industrial life. The span of her career complicates any account of Brazilian modernism as a single style. A painter could use what she had learned abroad while insisting that the resulting work answer to the geography, society and history in which she lived.

name: Frederick Douglass
summary: After escaping slavery, he used writing, public speaking and political organizing to fight for emancipation and citizenship.
biography:
Frederick Douglass was born into slavery in Maryland. Learning to read helped him gain access to arguments about rights that contradicted the conditions under which he lived. After escaping in 1838, he spoke at antislavery meetings and published a narrative of his life in 1845. The book let readers encounter his account in his own words. Douglass also helped sustain a newspaper, The North Star, that gave abolitionists a place to publish arguments and news between the public meetings where they encountered audiences in person.

During the Civil War he pressed the federal government to enlist Black soldiers and to recognize what their service meant for their claim to citizenship. His advocacy continued after emancipation when the status of freed people remained contested. He also supported women’s suffrage. Douglass’s life shows why abolishing slavery was only one part of a political project. The people who had secured their freedom still had to be able to speak, vote, work and exercise authority in public life.

name: W. E. B. Du Bois
summary: He combined social research, writing and international organizing to challenge racial hierarchy and document Black life.
biography:
W. E. B. Du Bois studied at Fisk and Harvard and conducted a detailed study of a Black community in Philadelphia. His research looked at households, work and neighborhoods, making it harder to explain inequality by treating African Americans as a single undifferentiated group. The book showed the importance of asking how institutions affected people’s choices. In The Souls of Black Folk he used essays and other literary forms to consider the experience of living in a country that excluded Black people while claiming them as citizens.

Du Bois helped organize the Niagara Movement and became a founding figure in the NAACP. As editor of The Crisis, he provided space to report on racial violence and to publish work by Black writers and artists. He also took part in organizing Pan-African congresses, connecting the question of racial equality in the United States to colonialism and self-government elsewhere. The breadth of his work matters because different kinds of argument were necessary. The evidence gathered by a researcher, the voice of an essayist and the reach of an organization could do different things for the same struggle.

name: Martin Luther King Jr.
summary: He helped organize nonviolent campaigns against segregation and for voting rights while pressing for economic justice.
biography:
Martin Luther King Jr. studied theology and became a Baptist minister. In Montgomery, Alabama, he was chosen to help lead the organization coordinating the city’s bus boycott. The boycott followed years of local organizing and would have failed without people who found ways to get to work and care for their families while staying off the buses. King’s speaking and negotiations gave the campaign a public voice, while the daily work of many others helped it endure.

He helped establish the Southern Christian Leadership Conference and worked with local groups on campaigns against segregation and for voting rights. His address at the March on Washington in 1963 reached a national audience, and he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964. In the following years he also spoke against the Vietnam War and pressed for economic changes that would improve the lives of poor people. King’s contribution is inseparable from the people who organized with him. His words helped campaigns address the public, but collective action gave those words their force.

name: Malcolm X
summary: He challenged white supremacy in speeches and organizing that increasingly connected Black freedom in the United States to human rights abroad.
biography:
Malcolm X, born Malcolm Little, became a member of the Nation of Islam during the years he spent in prison. After his release he became one of its most visible ministers. He called attention to violence and discrimination that many Americans discussed as if they were local exceptions. His work drew audiences who wanted to hear an argument for Black dignity and self-determination that did not begin by asking permission to make those claims.

In 1964 he broke with the Nation of Islam, traveled to Mecca and made further journeys in Africa and the Middle East. He reconsidered aspects of his earlier position on race while continuing to oppose white supremacy. The Organization of Afro-American Unity, which he helped establish, sought to put the civil rights struggle in an international human rights context. He was assassinated in 1965. The changes in his thinking matter as much as his most quoted lines. They show a political organizer adapting his ideas as new relationships and audiences changed the questions he could ask.

name: Medgar Evers
summary: As an NAACP field secretary, he took on the dangerous work of documenting racial violence and organizing in Mississippi.
biography:
Medgar Evers served in the U.S. Army during World War II and returned to Mississippi, where segregation narrowed the rights he could exercise at home. He attended Alcorn and took a job that brought him into contact with people around the state. As the NAACP’s Mississippi field secretary, he traveled widely to build membership and support local campaigns. Supporting a Black person attempting to register to vote or enroll in a segregated institution could require investigation, sustained contact and a willingness to put the effort before the public.

Evers documented racial violence and called attention to Mississippi’s failure to protect Black citizens. His family shared the risks created by the work. He was murdered outside his home in Jackson in 1963. Myrlie Evers and others continued pressing for justice, and the man who killed him was convicted decades later. The work Evers did before the assassination deserves attention in its own right. Organizing across a state where travel and public association could be dangerous meant creating the connections on which larger campaigns depended.

name: A. Philip Randolph
summary: He organized sleeping-car porters and used the prospect of mass protest to press for civil rights in employment.
biography:
A. Philip Randolph moved from Florida to New York and became involved in journalism, politics and labor organizing. The Pullman sleeping-car porters worked across a national rail network, but their hours, pay and job security were largely set by the company. Many were Black men who could not easily find another job if they were dismissed. Randolph helped lead their union through a long campaign for recognition. A contract in 1937 gave the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters a durable place in the collective bargaining system.

Before the United States entered World War II, Randolph threatened to bring a mass march to Washington unless the federal government addressed discrimination in defense employment. President Franklin Roosevelt issued an order banning such discrimination and creating a committee to address it. Randolph later helped lead the 1963 March on Washington with allies including Bayard Rustin. His career explains why the march included jobs in its demands. Civil rights needed to reach the places where people earned a living and the institutions that governed access to work.

name: Mary McLeod Bethune
summary: She built a school in Florida, founded a national women’s organization and pressed the federal government to address Black Americans’ needs.
biography:
Mary McLeod Bethune grew up in South Carolina in a family with few opportunities for formal schooling. After becoming a teacher, she founded a school for Black girls in Daytona, Florida, in 1904. Building it meant raising money, finding space and establishing a curriculum in a segregated city. The institution eventually became part of what is now Bethune-Cookman University. The work gave Bethune practical experience in how to stretch limited resources and build alliances without abandoning the needs of the people the school served.

Bethune carried those skills into national organizing. She founded the National Council of Negro Women and worked in the Roosevelt administration, where she pressed for Black youths to share in federal programs. She also helped bring Black advisers together across government offices. A school, an organization and a federal office offered different ways to act, and each could do something the others could not. Bethune’s career involved moving between those settings so that local experiences shaped national decisions and national resources reached local institutions.

name: Mary Church Terrell
summary: She used clubs, public speaking and legal pressure to challenge barriers that restricted Black women’s rights and access to public places.
biography:
Mary Church Terrell grew up in Memphis and studied at Oberlin College. She taught and became a public speaker, using the education available to her to make an argument for rights that were routinely denied to many Black women. In 1896 she became the founding president of the National Association of Colored Women, which gave local clubs a national organization. The work included addressing social needs and challenging the laws and customs that helped create them.

Terrell advocated for women’s suffrage while calling attention to racism in the suffrage movement itself. Decades later she took part in a campaign against segregated eating places in Washington, D.C. The campaign used evidence of older local laws prohibiting discrimination, and in 1953 the Supreme Court ruled that they were enforceable. Terrell participated in that fight near the end of her life. Her long career shows the different ways an exclusion can be challenged. Public argument could build support, an organization could sustain action, and a legal claim could force an institution to reckon with rules it had ignored.

name: Zitkála-Šá
place: United States and Yankton Dakota Nation
summary: The Yankton Dakota writer and organizer used stories, music and political advocacy to challenge forced assimilation.
biography:
Zitkála-Šá was born on the Yankton Dakota reservation and attended a boarding school that required Indigenous children to adopt unfamiliar language and customs. She wrote about those experiences in essays published for a national readership. The essays conveyed the perspective of a child experiencing an institution that claimed to know what was best for her. She also collected and retold Dakota stories, using writing to convey values and ideas that government schools were attempting to displace.

Her work was not limited to prose. She played violin and collaborated with composer William F. Hanson on The Sun Dance Opera. As an organizer she worked on political questions including citizenship and how the federal government handled Indigenous property. In 1926 she and her husband helped found the National Council of American Indians. Zitkála-Šá’s work crossed several forms because no one of them would have reached the same audience or accomplished the same task. She could give readers an individual account and still insist that the public address questions of collective rights and political power.

name: Wilma Mankiller
summary: She worked with Cherokee communities on local infrastructure and became the first woman to serve as principal chief of the Cherokee Nation.
biography:
Wilma Mankiller grew up in Oklahoma and moved with her family to California through a federal relocation program. Experiences with Indigenous organizing in the Bay Area shaped how she approached public work after returning to Oklahoma. She helped develop community projects for the Cherokee Nation. In Bell, residents worked together to bring running water to their homes. The project treated local knowledge and participation as resources rather than waiting for decisions to be made elsewhere.

Mankiller was elected deputy principal chief and became principal chief in 1985, the first woman to hold that office in the Cherokee Nation. She later won elections in her own right. Her administration pursued improvements in services such as health and education. These were matters of governance as well as programs for individual families. The ability to decide how services are delivered is a practical expression of a nation’s authority. Mankiller’s career shows how a project undertaken with one community can inform the larger work of governing and make public policy answer to the people who use it.
