name: Patsy Mink
summary: The Hawaiʻi congresswoman helped pass and defend Title IX protections against sex discrimination in education.
biography:
Patsy Takemoto Mink grew up in Hawaiʻi and studied law after facing barriers to entering medical school. She held elected office in Hawaiʻi before winning a seat in the U.S. House of Representatives in 1964. Her experience of exclusion helped shape her interest in the rules that determined who could study for a profession. Educational institutions that received federal funding could still use policies that shut people out based on sex, and a student might have little recourse against an admission or program rule.

Mink helped pass Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 and defended its reach during later disputes. The provision became especially visible in school sports, but its protection applies more widely to federally funded education programs. That broader scope reflects the range of barriers she and other legislators were addressing. Congress renamed the law in her honor after her death. Mink’s work illustrates the difference between opening the door of a particular school and establishing a rule that can be used by students at many institutions.

name: Yuri Kochiyama
summary: She built connections among struggles for Black freedom, Japanese American redress and the rights of political prisoners.
biography:
Yuri Kochiyama grew up in California and was incarcerated with her family during World War II under the federal policy that removed people of Japanese ancestry from the West Coast. After the war she moved to New York with her husband. In Harlem she saw how residents organized around issues that might seem separate to people outside the neighborhood. Her own experience of exclusion and confinement gave her a reason to listen and a basis for working with people whose histories differed from hers.

Kochiyama took part in Black freedom organizing, came to know Malcolm X and supported movements concerned with political prisoners and Puerto Rican independence. She also supported the effort to secure redress for Japanese American incarceration. She was often effective through the work of making and sustaining connections rather than by holding an elected position or leading a single national organization. Her papers and interviews preserve a view of activism organized through neighborhoods, meetings, correspondence and practical commitments to other people’s campaigns.

name: Grace Lee Boggs
summary: She helped organize around labor and civil rights in Detroit and later worked with young people on neighborhood projects.
biography:
Grace Lee Boggs, the daughter of Chinese immigrants, earned a doctorate in philosophy and found that a degree did not guarantee a teaching job. She became involved in organizing and moved to Detroit, where industrial work had shaped neighborhoods, migration and political life. With her husband James Boggs she took part in debates about labor, racism and what changes in manufacturing would mean for the people who had depended on it. Writing was one way to explore those questions, but both also took part in the organizations and relationships that gave the debates practical consequences.

Later in life Boggs helped establish Detroit Summer, a program that involved young people in rebuilding and tending neighborhoods. That work invited participants to learn by doing something that mattered to nearby residents. It also showed she was willing to change her account of what effective organizing looked like as the city changed. Her career connects two forms of work often treated separately: sustained reflection on what should change and sustained attention to the needs of the place where one lives.

name: Corazon Aquino
summary: She became president after the People Power uprising and oversaw the transition to the Philippines’ 1987 Constitution.
biography:
Corazon Aquino became a public figure after the assassination of her husband, opposition politician Benigno Aquino Jr., in 1983. The event widened opposition to Ferdinand Marcos and brought her into political activity that had not been her original career. She ran against Marcos in the February 1986 election. Disputes over the reported results combined with military defections and large civilian demonstrations to create a crisis for the government. Aquino took office after Marcos lost power.

Restoring a working constitutional system required choices beyond replacing the president. Her government arranged for a new constitution, which voters ratified in 1987. Her term also faced attempted coups and persistent social inequality. That record matters to understanding the People Power uprising because the mobilization that ended one government did not automatically settle what its successor could accomplish. Aquino’s part in the transition was to become the public focus of a coalition against authoritarian rule and then help establish institutions in which future political conflicts could be conducted.

name: Sirimavo Bandaranaike
summary: In 1960 she became the world’s first woman prime minister, beginning a political career that spanned three terms.
biography:
Sirimavo Bandaranaike entered party leadership after the assassination of her husband, Prime Minister Solomon Bandaranaike. Following the election of 1960 she became prime minister of Ceylon. She was the first woman to hold the office of prime minister in any country. Her political importance also rests on what her governments did, including efforts to expand state control in parts of the economy and pursue an independent course in international affairs. Those decisions unfolded as newly independent countries were defining how they would relate to the major powers.

During her second term Ceylon became a republic under the name Sri Lanka. Her governments’ choices about the structure of the state and the status of communities within it remained contested. She served again as prime minister in the 1990s, when her daughter Chandrika Kumaratunga was president and the office operated under a different constitutional arrangement. Bandaranaike’s career shows the need to distinguish a landmark election from the long political record that follows it. Becoming the first woman to enter the office opened a precedent, while governing exposed the consequences of particular policies.

name: Nanny of the Maroons
summary: She helped lead an independent Windward Maroon community that resisted British colonial rule in Jamaica.
biography:
Nanny was a leader of the Windward Maroons in eighteenth-century Jamaica. Maroon communities were formed by people who escaped enslavement and by their descendants. Establishing a settlement meant finding land that could be defended and where people could provide for themselves despite nearby plantations and the forces available to colonial authorities. Nanny Town, associated with her community, stood in the mountains of eastern Jamaica. The location helped its residents resist several British attacks during the 1730s.

Surviving colonial records are incomplete and were written by people who regarded the Maroons as opponents. Oral traditions preserve details about Nanny’s spiritual authority and leadership that the colonial record gives little room to. A grant from 1740 names Nanny and people associated with her. The document establishes part of her public role without telling us everything about her life, including her exact dates. Jamaica later recognized Nanny as a national hero. The records and traditions about her give different kinds of evidence for how one community made and defended an alternative to plantation slavery.

name: Nzinga
summary: She governed Ndongo and Matamba during a period of Portuguese expansion, combining diplomacy with military and political alliances.
biography:
Nzinga ruled in the region now called Angola during a period in which Portuguese officials and settlers were extending their influence and taking captives for the Atlantic slave trade. She traveled to Luanda in 1622 to negotiate on behalf of her brother, the ruler of Ndongo. That meeting was one stage in a long conflict over who could control people, trade and territory. She took power in Ndongo after his death and later established a political base in Matamba.

Nzinga worked with allies whose interests did not always coincide with hers. She changed diplomatic and military arrangements as the balance of power shifted, and at different points dealt with Dutch as well as Portuguese representatives. Her aim of sustaining a state did not make her rule an uncomplicated opposition to every form of enslavement; the societies involved were themselves entangled in systems of captivity and trade. Nzinga’s career shows that Central African rulers shaped events through their own decisions even when European records tended to describe them from the perspective of overseas empires.

name: Liliʻuokalani
summary: Hawaiʻi’s last reigning monarch resisted the loss of Hawaiian sovereignty and recorded the events in her own words.
biography:
Liliʻuokalani was educated in the Hawaiian Kingdom and became known as a composer as well as a member of its ruling family. She took the throne in 1891. The constitution imposed during her brother Kalākaua’s reign had reduced the monarch’s power and restricted access to political participation. Liliʻuokalani sought a new constitution, a proposal opposed by powerful residents with commercial and political interests tied to the United States. In 1893 opponents overthrew her government. She yielded authority under protest, hoping the United States would reverse what had occurred.

The monarchy was not restored. Liliʻuokalani continued to oppose annexation, and in 1898 she published an account of her life and the overthrow. That account let English-speaking readers encounter the dispute from the position of the sovereign whose authority had been removed. Her music preserves another kind of record, carrying Hawaiian words and melodies beyond particular political events. The two forms of work give later readers and listeners ways to understand the kingdom from within, rather than only through the decisions of the government that annexed it.

name: Murasaki Shikibu
summary: Her writing gave readers a view of the inner and social lives of people at Japan’s Heian court.
biography:
Murasaki Shikibu wrote in Japan during the Heian period, when court life gave a small group of women opportunities to write in Japanese. Her name as used today is a court name rather than a securely known personal name. She served Empress Shōshi and kept a diary that describes events and relationships in the imperial household. Her access to court did not mean she shared everyone’s perspective. Observations about written notes, visits and ceremonies record how much depended on people’s reading of social situations.

Her major work, The Tale of Genji, follows the fortunes of a prince and people connected to him across generations. It draws attention to the consequences of choices about rank, marriage and affection, including for characters with little ability to determine their own circumstances. Its long transmission through copies, new editions and illustrations reflects how later readers found different points of interest in it. The surviving work makes court life available through sustained attention to what people feel, what they can say and how they try to understand each other.

name: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
summary: Her poetry and prose explored what women could learn and how they could defend their right to study.
biography:
Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz grew up in New Spain and sought opportunities to read in a society where much formal education was closed to women. She spent time at the viceregal court before entering a convent. The convent offered time and space for study, although her work remained subject to religious authority. She wrote poems, plays and prose across several kinds of occasion. Her writing could entertain an audience and invite it to examine a difficult question at the same time.

A dispute over a theological argument led Sor Juana to write a reply in 1691 defending her intellectual life. The reply used examples and arguments rather than asking only for a personal exception: it considered how people could make judgments about women’s ability when women had so few opportunities to study. She died in 1695. Reading her work as part of New Spain’s literary culture helps explain both the range of her writing and the conditions it addresses. Her knowledge was visible to audiences that could admire it while still questioning her authority to use it.

name: Lakshmibai
summary: The ruler of Jhansi resisted British annexation and became a prominent leader during the uprising of 1857–58.
biography:
Lakshmibai became the rani of Jhansi through marriage to its ruler. After his death the British East India Company rejected the claim of their adopted son and annexed Jhansi under the policy often called the Doctrine of Lapse. She opposed the decision. The dispute concerned more than one family’s succession. It was an example of how the company was using its own rules about inheritance to expand control over Indian states and disregard local authority.

During the uprising that began in 1857, Lakshmibai took responsibility for defending Jhansi and later joined other forces resisting British rule. When Jhansi could no longer be held, she continued the campaign elsewhere and died near Gwalior in 1858. Accounts of her escape, appearance and last actions vary and have been elaborated in later retellings. The central political events are clearer. Her place in history comes from the connection between a dispute about who could rule Jhansi and a much wider struggle over the power of a commercial company to govern in India.

name: Yaa Asantewaa
summary: The queen mother of Ejisu helped lead Asante resistance when British authorities demanded the Golden Stool.
biography:
Yaa Asantewaa held the position of queen mother in Ejisu, a state within Asante. The office carried political responsibilities that included advising on questions of leadership. British authorities had exiled Asantehene Prempeh I and other leaders before demanding control of the Golden Stool. The stool represented the authority and collective identity of Asante. The demand was therefore understood as a challenge to the political order, not merely as a request to hand over a valuable object.

In 1900 Yaa Asantewaa helped rally resistance. Asante forces fought the British near Kumasi before the larger resources of the colonial military prevailed. The British exiled her to the Seychelles, where she died. Stories about her appeals to other leaders remain important in Ghana, although the exact words attributed to her cannot be treated as a transcript. The political role she occupied and the stakes of the conflict are well established. Her leadership shows how a person exercising authority through Asante institutions could resist an effort to redefine that authority as the property of an imperial government.

name: Leymah Gbowee
summary: She helped bring Christian and Muslim women together in a campaign for peace during Liberia’s civil war.
biography:
Leymah Gbowee worked with people affected by years of war in Liberia and became involved in organizing for peace. A particular difficulty was bringing together people whose daily lives and places of worship had often been separated. The Women of Liberia Mass Action for Peace drew on cooperation among Christian and Muslim women. Participants gathered publicly and made demands on leaders to reach a settlement. Their visibility in public required consistent work: a protest that needed people from different communities to return day after day depended on trust and a shared purpose.

Gbowee and other organizers brought pressure to bear during peace talks in Ghana. The settlement in 2003 depended on decisions by many parties, but the women’s campaign made it harder for negotiators to disregard the people most affected by delay. Gbowee shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 2011 with Ellen Johnson Sirleaf and Tawakkol Karman. Her work showed how a coalition can act effectively when participants do not need to have the same beliefs or backgrounds to agree on what their leaders must do.

name: Shirin Ebadi
summary: She used legal practice and public advocacy to defend women, children and others whose rights were restricted in Iran.
biography:
Shirin Ebadi trained as a lawyer and became a judge in Iran before the revolution of 1979. She attained a senior position in a Tehran court. After the revolution, changes to the judiciary prevented her and other women from continuing to exercise the same authority. She later practiced as a lawyer, bringing knowledge of how courts operate to a different role. In cases involving women, children and political defendants, doing the work could require challenging practices of institutions that were also supposed to protect people.

Ebadi also helped build organizations for legal and human rights work. In 2003 she became the first Iranian recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize. International recognition gave her work a wider audience without resolving the legal and political obstacles she described. Her career makes the distinction between a right stated in general terms and the means to claim it in a particular case. Lawyers, institutions and people willing to bring a case are all needed before a promise of protection can be tested in court.

name: Tawakkol Karman
summary: She organized for press freedom and took a prominent role in Yemen’s 2011 protest movement.
biography:
Tawakkol Karman worked in journalism in Yemen and helped establish Women Journalists Without Chains in 2005. Its organizing grew out of a practical question: if reporters are prevented from gathering or publishing news, people may not learn what officials have done or what has happened to other citizens. Working on press freedom therefore brought Karman into contact with a wider set of grievances about public authority. She took part in repeated demonstrations before protests spread across the region in 2011.

In Yemen that year she became one of the most visible participants in demonstrations calling for political change. Her organizing included insisting that women had a place in public protest and debate. Karman shared the 2011 Nobel Peace Prize with Ellen Johnson Sirleaf and Leymah Gbowee. A prize given during a period of upheaval could draw attention to the work without determining the political future of Yemen. Karman’s earlier journalism activism helps explain what protest participants were seeking beyond a change of leaders: the ability to report events, organize and speak in public.
